In her speech to the town meeting, Marguerite Osgood tries to convince the council to vote down the rezoning by presenting herself as a practical person who knows the harbor, and then by redefining the north wharf as something the whole town needs instead of just a business that is losing money. She does this through a metaphor, a concession, and a story about a rescue, which together move the audience from thinking about money to thinking about what kind of town they want.

Osgood begins by building her credibility. She says "I am not a planner, a developer, or an economist. I am a woman who knows where the rocks are." By listing what she is not, she sounds humble and not like someone with an agenda, and the line about the rocks makes her sound like she has real experience. This matters because the audience is about to vote on a developer's plan, and she needs them to trust her over a glossy brochure. She also describes the brochure's pictures as having "not a single forklift, fuel barge, or crab pot," which points out what the developer left out and makes the audience notice what would be lost.

Next, Osgood makes a concession. She admits "The fishing fleet is smaller than it was" and that the ice house closed, and she says condominium taxes are "real money." This helps her because the people who want the tax money will not feel attacked, and it makes her seem fair and honest. Then she uses her metaphor: "It is not a gold mine. It is a kitchen." The kitchen idea works because everyone understands that a restaurant needs a kitchen even if the kitchen does not make money by itself. She then lists the mechanic, the welder, and the net patcher, and says "half of you" buy boots at the supply store, which speaks directly to the people in the room. The statistics about four million dollars and one hundred and forty jobs back this up and show the wharf is important to the economy.

The most powerful part is probably the Anna Belle story. Osgood changes her tone to say "something now that is harder to put in a brochure," and tells how Dale Cuttery got to the trawler in eleven minutes. Her short sentences, "It cannot. Nobody is aboard," make the point very clearly. This shows the wharf is also about safety and not only about money, which is something the condominiums can't replace.

Finally, she asks "what are we really deciding?" and says the waterfront will either "belong to the town or merely faces it." Her ending goes back to her piloting job by saying she wants to "bring one town in too," and she offers to help find another way to pay for the culvert. This shows she is not just saying no but is willing to help. Overall, Osgood persuades by being trustworthy, fair, and by making the audience see the wharf differently.

When a retired harbor pilot stands up at a town meeting to defend the old pier, some people in the room have probably already decided she is being nostalgic. Marguerite Osgood seems to know this. Instead of fighting the developer's money argument head on, she gives the council most of it, then quietly changes what the argument is about. By building her credibility as a practical insider, conceding the wharf's financial weakness, and redefining the wharf first as a "kitchen" and then as a lifeline, Osgood makes a no vote look like the hardheaded choice rather than the sentimental one.

Osgood's opening is built to head off the charge that she is just attached to the past. She describes her job in physical terms, climbing "a rope ladder up the side of other people's ships," and then lists what she is not: "a planner, a developer, or an economist." This could sound like a weakness, but she turns it around with "I am a woman who knows where the rocks are." The rocks are literal, but they also hint that she sees dangers the brochure doesn't. She sets herself up as the person who has seen the channel, not the drawings, which matters in a room about to vote based on drawings.

That is exactly where she goes next. Rather than attacking the developers, she compliments the brochure ("It is handsome") and then points to what is missing from it: "not a single forklift, fuel barge, or crab pot." Osgood uses the developer's own picture as her evidence. The council has probably been looking at these renderings for weeks, and she asks them to see the empty space in them. "That absence is the point of the drawing" is almost an accusation, but it is phrased so calmly that nobody can call it one.

The most important move in the speech is the concession in paragraph three. Osgood lists the bad news herself: the ice house closed, the fuel dock "loses money three months a year," and the town "cannot fix the culvert on Pell Street." By naming the culvert she shows she understands why a council member might vote yes, and she admits she would deserve to be laughed "out of the room" if she called the wharf a gold mine. Because she already gave up the unflattering numbers, the four million dollars of catch and "one hundred and forty jobs" in paragraph four sound like an honest count instead of a sales pitch. The kitchen metaphor does the real work. A kitchen isn't judged by whether it makes money alone, and "try running a restaurant without one" lets the audience see the mechanic, the welder and the net mender as parts of one system. The chain of "Then the mechanic goes. Then the welder." gets shorter each time, so the town seems to shrink as the sentences do, until even the kids leave.

Then Osgood says she wants to say something "harder to put in a brochure," and the speech shifts from economics to safety. Placing the Anna Belle story after the statistics is smart. If she had opened with it, it might seem like a tearjerker; coming after the numbers, it shows what the numbers can't measure. The key line is "They were there in eleven minutes because they were already there." The point is not really that fishermen are heroes but that they are physically present on the water. Her short sentences, "It cannot. Nobody is aboard," are almost flat, which makes the empty marina feel colder than any adjective could.

Osgood asks whether the waterfront "belongs to the town or merely faces it," and she closes by returning to her own job, hoping "to help bring one town in too." The piloting image loops back to the rope ladder in her first sentence, so her whole career becomes the argument. Her last line offers to "find another way to pay for the culvert," which keeps her from sounding like someone who just says no. Schools should require a hand craft, but only for a short time and only if the class is taught as a way of learning to deal with mistakes, not as job training. A full year of ninety hours for every student is probably too much, but a single semester or a unit in the middle grades is worth the cost.

The parents in Pellingham are right that ninety hours is ninety hours. A student who wants to go into engineering could use that time on statistics or coding, and it is hard to say a wobbly chair is more useful than that. But I think the board chair is also right that the requirement is not about chairs. In my own life, I took a half-year shop class in ninth grade where we had to build a small wooden toolbox. Mine came out crooked because I cut one side too short, and there was no way to fix it. I had to either start over with new wood or live with it. In math class, I can erase a wrong answer, and on a computer I can press undo, but the board I cut was just cut. That moment taught me to measure twice, which sounds like a cliche, but I actually do it now when I do other things like planning out an essay or packing for a trip.

This shows why a short requirement can be worth it even when machines do manual work better. The point is not to compete with a factory. The point is that students rarely get to experience a mistake that stays a mistake. Most of school lets you redo things, so a craft class fills a gap that other classes leave empty. A student who never gets that experience may be less careful, or at least may not understand why careful people are careful.

However, this is also why I think a full year is too long. Once a student has felt the lesson, more hours probably give less. My cousin spent a whole year in an auto shop and said he learned the main idea in the first couple of months and the rest was repetition. If he had wanted to be a mechanic that would be fine, but then it is an elective, not a requirement. So I would limit the requirement to one semester and let students who like it continue by choice.

Some people would say a requirement makes kids resent the craft, and that may be true for some. But many students would never try woodworking or bookbinding on their own, so a small push is how they find out whether they like it. In conclusion, schools should require a short hand craft course focused on consequences, and leave the rest to students who want more.

In eighth grade I glued up a maple cutting board with the grain running the wrong way, and three weeks later it split down the middle on my mom's counter. Nobody had to grade it. The board graded itself. I thought about that board while reading about the parents in Pellingham, because they are right that a machine could have made a better one in a minute. But they are missing what the crack taught me. Schools should require a hand craft, but only if it is taught as practice in living with mistakes that cannot be undone, not as a weak copy of factory training, and only if students get to choose the craft and the requirement is shorter than a full year.

The parents' best argument is about time, and it deserves a real answer. My friend Marcus wants to study computer science, and ninety more hours of coding would probably get him one more finished project for his portfolio. That matters. But the thing that makes coding easy to practice is also what limits it as a teacher. When Marcus breaks his program he hits Ctrl-Z or goes back to an earlier version, and the mistake disappears like it never happened. When I made my second board I measured three times before every cut, not because Mr. Halloran told me to, but because I had already watched one split. Coding and statistics teach students to be correct eventually. They are worse at teaching students to be careful beforehand, because they forgive too easily. A craft class gives Marcus something his other ninety hours can't.

It is also not true that manual judgment has vanished just because machines exist. The mechanic at the bike shop near my house trues wheels by spinning them and plucking the spokes like guitar strings, listening for the one that sounds flat. The shop owns a truing stand that measures automatically, but he told me it "doesn't know when the rim itself is bent." What he has isn't really speed or precision, since the machine beats him at both. What he has is the habit of noticing. That is why I think both sides in Pellingham are measuring the wrong thing when they talk about the chair. The parents treat the wobbling chair as a failure because a factory chair is better. But a factory chair can't tell you anything about the person who made it, and a wobbling chair is a record of exactly where the student's attention slipped. The point of the class is the wobble.

The parents also assume that school time is a fixed budget that should be spent on what students will "actually need." The problem is that nobody is very good at predicting that. My grandmother's high school required shorthand because every office supposedly needed it, and twenty years later the skill was useless. Some of the coding languages being pushed today may be written mostly by AI before current juniors finish college. If schools can't guess which skills will last, it makes more sense to spend some time on habits that carry over, like patience and taking responsibility for your own mistakes, than to spend every hour betting on the job market.

Still, there is a tension inside my own position. Part of why my cutting board meant something is that I wanted it to turn out well. A student forced into weaving who doesn't care will just put in the hours, and a box-checking requirement could kill the exact attention it is supposed to build. That is why the conditions matter. Students should pick their own craft, the class should be one semester, and grading should reward the reflection on what went wrong, not a polished final product. Pellingham's board chair said the requirement "is not about chairs." She's right, but the school has to actually teach it that way, or the parents will be right too.

Everyone in the Pellingham argument seems to agree on one thing: the student's chair will wobble, and that is bad. The parents think the wobble proves the ninety hours were wasted, and even the board chair treats it as a small price for some deeper lesson. I think the wobble is the lesson. Schools should require a hand craft, but only as a one-semester course that students choose and that is graded on how they respond to their mistakes, not on how good the final object looks. Taught as job training, the requirement deserves the parents' objections. Taught as practice in living with consequences, it gives students something a statistics course can't.

I know this because of a cutting board. In eighth grade I glued maple and walnut strips together in Mr. Halvorsen's shop class, and I was so impatient that I tightened the clamps on one side before the other. The board dried with a bow in it, maybe a quarter inch. On a computer I would have hit undo. Instead I had to choose between planing it flat, which would make it thinner than the plan called for, or starting over and losing two weeks. I planed it. It is thin and a little uneven and my mom still uses it for bread. What I learned was not how to make a cutting board, since a factory does that better, but how to make a decision after the fact, when every option costs something. Almost no other class makes me practice that, because in almost every other class the wrong answer just gets erased.

The parents' strongest point is that ninety hours is ninety hours, and I don't want to wave it away. But the objection depends on two assumptions: that we know which skills students will "actually need," and that time spent on one thing is simply subtracted from another. The first assumption has a bad track record. When my brother was a freshman, his school pushed everyone into intro coding because it was supposedly the safest skill in the economy. Now he's in college and says AI tools write most of the routine code he was taught to write. What turned out to matter was debugging, figuring out why something broke and what to do with the version he already had. That is closer to my warped cutting board than to anything on a list of "future skills."

The second assumption is shakier than it sounds too. My uncle runs a small auto repair shop, and his diagnostic computer reads error codes faster than he ever could. But he told me the computer only tells him where to look; he still has to listen to the engine and decide whether a part needs replacing or whether the customer can live with it another year. That judgment didn't come from a separate pile of hours. It came from working with his hands, and it makes his use of the machine better, not worse. Shop hours aren't always subtracted from technical learning. Sometimes they are what makes it stick.

There is a real problem with my own position, though. Part of why the cutting board mattered is that I cared about it, and a requirement risks turning craft into one more box to check. That is why I would keep it to one semester, let students pick the craft, and base the grade on a short reflection about what went wrong and what they did about it. A required class can't force anyone to care, but it can put them in a room where a mistake can't be erased. The wobbling chair isn't the failure of the requirement. A student who never makes one would be.
